evidence.title: A Novel Playbook for Pragmatic Trial Operations to Monitor and Evaluate Ambient Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice
evidence.effect: Documentation accuracy recovered from 35% to the 79% baseline following user training and note template redesign.
evidence.quote: A brief workflow issue related to a note template change initially reduced ICD-10 documentation accuracy from 79% (95% confidence interval [CI], 72 to 86%) to 35% (95% CI, 28 to 42%); accuracy returned to baseline after note template redesign and user training.

evidence.title: Don’t set and forget: Optimising Digital Early Warning Tools through upgrade and evaluation
evidence.outcome: Clinician awareness of tool functionality and training needs after upgrade
evidence.effect: Focus groups and surveys identified lack of awareness of specific functionality and need for training after the DEWT upgrade; mental state documentation reduced post-upgrade.
evidence.quote: Stakeholder focus groups and surveys identified a lack of awareness of specific functionality, issues with alert fatigue, technical challenges with the system, the need for training and concerns around over-reliance on the system by junior staff.

commentary.bottom_line: One quasi-experimental study of 66 providers found that ICD-10 documentation accuracy recovered from 35% to its 79% baseline after user training combined with note template redesign, and a hazard study found that clinicians lacked awareness of specific functionality after a tool upgrade. The evidence suggests that retraining after updates may restore performance, but certainty is very low because a single study with a co-intervention tests the practice.

perspectives.view: Only one study tests the practice, and it uses a quasi-experimental design rather than randomization. Training was paired with template redesign, so the effect of training alone cannot be isolated. Documentation accuracy is a surrogate outcome, and a single sample of 66 providers limits precision. These limitations support a very low certainty rating.

After an upgrade across 15 Australian hospitals, clinicians lacked awareness of specific functions and mental state documentation fell. This finding shows that updates can degrade how a tool is used. In the United States study, accuracy recovered from 35% to the 79% baseline after intervention, which suggests a refresh may correct decline, though the study did not measure patient harm.

The recovery in the United States study followed both user training and a redesigned note template, which suggests that workflow changes and education may need to be delivered together. The supplied findings do not describe how long gains lasted, how much staff time training required, or how update triggers were detected in practice.

The tested intervention combined training with template changes for 66 providers. The supplied finding includes no cost, staffing hours, or scheduling data, so leaders cannot use this evidence to estimate the burden of triggering retraining after every material update across a large workforce.

The supplied study descriptions do not indicate whether the providers or patients involved came from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Whether retraining after updates performs differently in under-resourced settings, where training time may be scarcer, remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study isolates the effect of retraining or competency reassessment from concurrent workflow or template changes, and none reports patient outcomes, durability of recovered performance, or the cost of update-triggered training. Studies are also needed for tool retirement and disabled features, which no supplied study examines.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither the testing study nor the hazard study is described as including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that the reported recovery in documentation accuracy will transfer to their settings.
